We are interested in finding strucutre in the similar patterns that the stock series take. Without rescaling each, the differences we see between the series will be mostly due to the fact that they have different means and variances. The differences among the means and variances are largely due the fact that different stocks sell at different prices, and are not of interest.

In [6]:
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
In [7]:
pcaout = PCA(n_components=15)
pcaout.fit(data)
plt.plot(range(1,16),pcaout.explained_variance_ratio_)
plt.xlabel('component', size=12)
plt.ylabel('proportion of variance explained', size=12)
plt.show()

From the scree plot, we see that there is a fall in the proportion of variance explained, but it's not so sharp as to suggest a clear point at which we have separated signal from noise. If one were using this for dimension reduction, a reasonable argument could be made for using from 3 to 6 components.

The PCA has enabled a significant reduction in dimensionality in this case (from 30 to fewer than 10 dimensions), but the lack of a clear break in the scree plot makes it a little tricky. If we look at the proportion of variance explained by each component, then we see that it takes seven components to explain 85% of the variability and 11 components to explain 90%.

In [8]:
print(sum(pcaout.explained_variance_ratio_[:7]))
print(sum(pcaout.explained_variance_ratio_[:11]))

0.8495655602452233
0.9094770526573452

Ultimately, whether or not this dimension reduction is effective will depend on how it is utilized. But, these results suggest that we are not achieving an ideal compression with PCA.

Question 2¶

In [9]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from mpl_toolkits.mplot3d import Axes3D

from sklearn import manifold, datasets

n_points = 1000
Scurve, Scolor = datasets.make_s_curve(n_points, random_state=0)

Here we recreate the S curve, but with added noise.

In [10]:
Snoise = Scurve + \
   np.matrix(np.random.normal(0,.3,3000)).\
   reshape(1000,3)

Now, use isomap to find a lower dimensional representation. If you manipulate the tuning parameter (the number of nearest neighbors), it is possible to reach a representation that does an OK job of finding the one-dimensional structure in the S curve. See below for the case where the tuning parameter is set to three.

In [11]:
#Isomap of Snoise
Y = manifold.Isomap(n_neighbors=3, 
    n_components=2).fit_transform(Snoise)

plt.scatter(Y[:, 0], Y[:, 1], c=Scolor, 
   cmap=plt.cm.Spectral)
plt.title("Results from Isomap")
plt.show()

If we try the same level of noise with diffusion map (again after some manipulation of the tuning parameter), we see a more clear evolution along the X axis, although it is not perfect.

In [12]:
from pydiffmap import diffusion_map as dm

dmap = dm.DiffusionMap.from_sklearn(n_evecs=3, epsilon=1)
Scurvediffmap = dmap.fit_transform(Snoise)

plt.scatter(Scurvediffmap[:, 0], 
   Scurvediffmap[:, 1], c=Scolor, 
   cmap=plt.cm.Spectral)
plt.title("Results from Diffusion Map")
plt.show()

dfsmo['sector'].fillna("None",inplace=True)
In [25]:
import seaborn as sns
dfsmo['iso1'] = Y[:,0]
dfsmo['iso2'] = Y[:,1]
dfsmo['iso3'] = Y[:,2]
dfsmo['iso4'] = Y[:,3]
dfsmo['iso5'] = Y[:,4]
In [26]:
sns.set(rc={'figure.figsize':(9,9)})

ax = sns.scatterplot(x="iso1", y="iso2", data=dfsmo, s=30, hue="sector")
plt.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 1.0))
plt.xlabel("First Isomap Coordinate")
plt.ylabel("Second Isomap Coordinate")
plt.show()
In [27]:
import plotly.express as px
dfsmo['name'] = list(stock_name)
fig = px.scatter_3d(dfsmo, x='iso1', y='iso2', z='iso3', hover_name="name",color="sector", opacity=0.7)
fig.show()

The two-dimensional projection does not reveal much of a relationship with sector, but that is not too surprising. We could explore more by looking a points close together and comparing their time series shapes. We should see that points close in this space have similar shapes.

We could also take advantage of clustering, as shown below, to get at the same behavior.

4. Clustering of Smoothed Series¶

First, we just sample 100 of the series and inspect the dendrogram produced by hierarchical clustering.

In [28]:
df2 = dfsmo.copy()

df2.drop(columns=['sector','iso1','iso2','iso3','iso4','iso5'],
    axis=1,inplace=True)

df2sub = df2.sample(100)

stock_name = df2sub['name']
df2sub.drop(['name'], axis=1, inplace=True)

The dendrogram is created below.

In [29]:
from scipy.cluster import hierarchy
hcout = hierarchy.linkage(df2sub, method="complete")
fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 1, figsize=[7,20])

labs = pd.array(stock_name).astype("str")
hierarchy.dendrogram(hcout,ax=axs,orientation="left",labels=labs,leaf_font_size=12)
None

Note that this dendrogram shows pairs of series that are close together, much closer than when we used the original series (in lecture). The reason is that the original series are dominated by noise, and the distance measure is contaiminated by that noise: Pairs of series that are "close," in the sense that their underlying shapes are similar, are still judged to be distant because of the noise.

The result gives us much more confidence that we are actually recovering useful clusters by using the smoothed series.

Let's now revisit the isomap analysis of above. We will repeat the clustering, but this time using the entire data set.

In [30]:
stock_name = df2['name']
df2.drop(['name'], axis=1, inplace=True)
hcoutfull = hierarchy.linkage(df2, method="complete")

We add onto the data frame dfsmo a column corresponding to the cluster label.

In [31]:
dfsmo['clust'] = hierarchy.fcluster(hcoutfull,t=5,criterion="maxclust")

Now recreate the plot, but this time color by the cluster label.

In [32]:
sns.set(rc={'figure.figsize':(9,9)})

ax = sns.scatterplot(x="iso1", y="iso2", data=dfsmo, s=30, hue="clust")
plt.legend(bbox_to_anchor=(1.0, 1.0))
plt.xlabel("First Isomap Coordinate")
plt.ylabel("Second Isomap Coordinate")
plt.show()

What we see here is that series that the clustering identified as being similar are indeed being plotted in close proximity in this two-dimensional represetation.
